rationale: The BOOK ENTRY makes a minimal metonymic identification: a voice is the words of the one speaking, and specifically the Shepherd's voice in John 10:27 is Christ's words/teaching. John 10:27 ('My sheep hear my voice... and they follow me') carries this directly: what the sheep hear and follow is what Christ says. The chapter reinforces the mechanics with John 10:5 — the sheep 'know not the voice of strangers,' where refusing a voice can only mean refusing what the stranger says, i.e., his words or teaching. The strongest counter-reading — the common interpretation that 'voice' symbolizes divine self-revelation, presence, and authoritative communication demanding obedience — does not contradict this core; it is the same referent stated at a broader thematic level. God's authoritative communication just is His words being spoken and heard. A broader label is not a rival core identification under the governing standard. No text supplied is better explained by the broader abstraction than by the concrete 'voice = the speaker's words' reading; indeed the following/obeying response in John 10:27 presupposes propositional content (words) rather than mere presence or power. Both printed clauses of the entry are supported, so the scope is FULL.
book_core_identification: 'Voice' denotes the words of the one speaking; in John 10:27 the Shepherd's (Christ's) voice is His words — His spoken teaching that the sheep hear and follow.
book_secondary_elaborations: The specific application clause 'the Shepherd's voice is His words,' anchoring the general definition to John 10:27 (this is the entry's own instance of its core, and it is supported by John 10:27 and 10:3-5).
chapter_only_objections: The chapter's claim that 'the stranger' in John 10:5 specifically means 'one outside the covenant' is a further identification not asserted in the glossary entry and not independently demonstrated here.

The chapter's larger thesis that knowing God is a covenant bond proven by commandment-keeping (built from 1 John 2:3-4, Amos 3:2, Genesis 4:1, etc.) is a chapter-level argument, not part of the printed entry.
The chapter's equations sheep = His people and name = a symbol with its own chapter are separate glossary claims outside this entry's scope.
The chapter's readings of love/faith/belief/works (e.g., John 3:36 obedience contrast, hate as un-choosing) are chapter-level doctrinal arguments not under judgment here.
strongest_counter_interpretation: The common interpretation exemplified by Responses A–D: 'voice' — especially 'the voice of the LORD' or 'a voice from heaven' — symbolizes God's direct self-revelation, presence, power, and authoritative communication that calls for hearing and obedience, with the Shepherd's voice in John 10 functioning as relational guidance and recognition marking belonging to His flock.
counter_core_identification: Voice = divine self-revelation and authoritative communication (God's or Christ's communicative presence demanding a response of hearing and obedience).
material_core_denial: None. The counter does not deny that a voice consists of the speaker's words; 'authoritative communication' and 'revelation' are broader thematic descriptions of the same referent — the words God or Christ speaks. Both identifications can be true of the same referent in John 10:27, so no material core denial exists.
counter_case: 'Voice' across Scripture is a broad theophanic motif (Psalm 29; Exodus 19; Matthew 3:17) signifying presence and power, not merely lexical 'words.'
In John 10 the emphasis is relational recognition — the sheep know the voice — suggesting personal identification of the speaker, not only the content of speech.
Some 'voice' texts (thunder in Psalm 29; sound like many waters in Revelation 1:15) foreground non-verbal power, which 'words' alone may seem too narrow to cover.
book_explanatory_advantages: It explains the response mechanics of John 10:27: sheep 'follow' the voice, and following requires propositional content — commands and teaching — which 'words' supplies and bare 'presence' or 'power' does not.
It explains John 10:5 cleanly: refusing to follow the stranger's voice means refusing the stranger's words/teaching; 'presence' cannot be followed or refused in this sense.

It is a precise, testable metonymy consistent with the book's stated method (define the symbol by what the texts require), whereas the counter's 'revelation/presence/authority' is a thematic abstraction layered on top of the same fact that a voice conveys words.

Even the counter responses' own primary bases (Deuteronomy 4:12: 'ye heard the voice of the words'; Hebrews 3:7-15: hearing His voice = heeding what is said) reduce to hearing and obeying spoken words.
counter_explanatory_advantages: It better foregrounds theophanic-power passages (Psalm 29 thunder; Revelation 1:15 many waters) where the sensory force of the voice, not its verbal content, is emphasized — but none of those passages are printed with this entry, and the entry does not deny them.
It captures the recognition/identity dimension of John 10 (knowing whose voice it is), though this is compatible with the voice being the speaker's words.
decisive_sources: John 10:27 (KJV excerpt printed with the entry)
John 10:3-5 as deployed in the supporting chapter (the stranger's voice the sheep will not follow)
Chapter 6's explicit derivation: 'the voice is His words, and to know that voice is to follow it'
unresolved_objections: The entry's definition, applied universally, would need supplementation for purely theophanic 'voice' texts (e.g., thunder imagery in Psalm 29), but no such text is printed with this entry and the definition is not falsified by them — a voice of thunder still communicates from the speaker.
